newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Twilight - empire Britons work as HK "white coolies".
newsitem.headline: Twilight - empire Britons work as HK "white coolies".

text.p: The British even work as shoeshine boys in this affluent Chinese metropolis.
From downtown bars to fish and chip shops, the odds are you will be served by a backpacker on a round-the-world tour who could not resist the lure of a Hong Kong stopover.

In a unique role reversal in the dying days of Empire, the young Britons who take the barman, waitress, delivery and construction jobs spurned by the Chinese are dubbed "The last of the white coolies."
Others in this capitalist goldmine where the young colonials make half the average Chinese wage bluntly call them FILTH -- Failed in London, Try Hong Kong.
But all that will come to an end with the handover to China of Britain's last Asian colony on June 30.
Young Britons in thousands of low-paid jobs fled the colony at the end of March -- but only briefly as they scrabbled in a mass exodus to win a year's breathing space.
They lost the right from April 1 to work in Hong Kong without an entry visa or work permit.
So, to beat the deadline, they went on quick trips to the neighbouring Portuguese territory of Macau and returned to gain one precious last 12-month residency stamp.
Freckle-faced waitress Emily Knapp, 24, is typical of this new breed of accidental tourist.

Taking a brief break from her job in the Post '97 restaurant, she said: "I was backpacking in Southeast Asia round Cambodia and Vietnam. I was running out of money and coming to the end of my funds. I got offered three jobs in the same day."

She is staying for the handover celebrations in Lan Kwai Fong, a backstreet yuppie enclave where dark-suited young executives quaff designer beers and whisky sours in people-watching bars where poseurs abound.
Next stop for Knapp is a job in China as a language teacher before she resumes her travels.
Vivacious Liverpudlian Karen O'Neill, 28, told a similar tale: "I had a round-the-world ticket with seven countries left on it but I loved it so much I never got past Hong Kong."
But she too is ready to hit the road. "I am off to Spain to open a restaurant there with my Mum and Dad."
Nichole Garnaut's '97 Group runs six bars, restaurants and nightclubs in Hong Kong. They have a staff of 250. About 60 percent of those are expatriate staff.
Finding Chinese local staff is an uphill climb: "The jobs are not really well enough paid for them and it is really difficult to get them."

"We are a little bit more Western in our approach. Maybe they don't feel comfortable," she said, sipping champagne in the La Dolce Vita bar as the evening noise level reaches a crescendo among the pony tails and power dressers just 11 days away from a new life under Chinese rulers.
